text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
The man who founded the colonies of New South Wales and Norfolk Island, ARTHUR PHILLIP, was born in 1738. The English Naval commander headed a home guard defence force in retirement.
The English inventor of the steel pen-nib JOSEPH GILLOT was born in 1799.

American food manufacturer HENRY HEINZ was born in 1844. He was superstitious, and even though he had developed 60 varieties when his product slogan was introduced, he selected 57 because of its numerological significance.
Australian zoologist THEODORE FLYNN was born in 1883. He was the father of actor ERROL FLYNN.
Argentinian general and president JUAN PERON was born in 1895. He was deposed in 1955 and returned to office in 1973.
British molecular biologist CESAR MILSTEIN was born in 1927. He shared a Nobel Prize in 1984 for his work on techniques to produce antibodies, in order to immunise against specific diseases.
Welsh-born world professional snooker champion RAY REARDON was born in 1932. He was champion in 1970 and from 1973 to 1976.

Australian radio and TV quiz champion and federal minister BARRY JONES was born in 1932. He was a pioneer of radio talkback. As a cabinet minister he was responsible for establishing the Commission for the Future.
Australian radio star GARRY O'CALLAGHAN was born in 1933. He gained attention as the only radio journalist to cover the escape of Mrs PETROV from Soviet agents in the 1950s spy case.
American politician and black civil rights campaigner REVEREND JESSE JACKSON was born in 1941.
United States bass player and founder of 'Kool and the Gang', ROBERT BELL, was born in 1950. Hits included "Jungle Boogie" (1973) and "Hollywood Swinging" (1974).
** EVENTS **
1871 : The great fire of Chicago started, causing
hundreds to flee their homes.
1925 : Australia's Dame NELLIE MELBA announced her
retirement.
1932 : The London Philharmonic Orchestra gave its first
performance.
1947 : On a visit to New Zealand, RANDOLPH CHURCHILL said
the "prize for slowness" went to New Zealand waterside workers.
1952 : A British rail crash in Harrow, involving three
trains, killed 112 and injured another 200 passengers.
1957 : Singer JERRY LEE LEWIS recorded "Great Balls of
Fire" at the Sun Studios in Memphis.
1965 : Britain's tallest building to date opened.
The Post Office Tower contained a revolving restaurant and viewing galleries.
1967 : The breathalyser was used for the first time in
Britain. The suspect was a speeding motorist in Somerset.
1973 : The first legal commercial radio station in
Britain (London Broadcasting) went to air.
1981 : Treasure worth 83 million dollars was retrieved

from the Barents Sea. The 431 gold bars had lain on the sea bed for almost 40 years. They were part of the cargo on the British cruiser "Edinburgh" which was sunk in May 1942. The ship was transporting the bullion from Russia to Britain when she became involved in a battle with German destroyers and a U-boat. It took ten divers three weeks to recover the treasure. The salvage companies received 45 percent of the value of the gold, with the remainder going to the British and Soviet governments.
1989 : A Tourism industry report claimed the Australian
pilots' strike had cost the industry 340 million dollars in cancellations.
1994 : Iraqi troops began advancing on Kuwait, causing

the United States and other Gulf allies to rush forces to the region. Three days later the Iraqi troops started to withdraw from their positions near the Kuait border, after threats of military action from the United States.
